problem: End-to-end ImageNav methods encode goal and observation images into separate semantic feature vectors and leave the comparison to the policy network. These vectors carry no accurate direction information, so the agent takes superfluous actions, and performance drops when the goal image is captured from a different viewpoint than the agent's (the user-matched setting).
motivation: Humans navigate by reasoning about the spatial relationship between the current view and the goal, which yields orientation cues. Relationships between images depend less on detailed semantics and so are less sensitive to viewpoint mismatch. Real users will not photograph goals from the agent's camera pose, so robustness to this mismatch matters for deployment.
key_idea: Replace separate semantic features with explicit goal-observation correlations (dense cross-correlation, then a multi-scale, direction-aware lookup on a correlation pyramid) as the input to the policy network.
insight: Explicit correlation cues are more useful than richer semantic features. A minimalist two-score correlation already beats the vector baseline (Table 4: SR 22.6 vs 16.2), and the dense correlation raises SPL/SR from 16.1/22.6 to 53.2/79.4. Ablations show that both cross-correlation and fine-grained correlation are needed (Table 5), and that the lookup helps only with a 16x16 feature map (Table 6). More pyramid layers add gains (SPL 58.0 → 59.4 → 61.2), and the advantage over FGPrompt grows under viewpoint mismatch.
method: Perception: a weight-sharing ResNet-9 trained from scratch encodes the goal image and the current RGB image into feature vectors or feature maps (128x128 input).
Minimalist Relationship: two feature vectors per image, with receptive fields covering the left and right halves. Their dot products give a 2-dim correlation cue.
Dense Relationship: 4x4 feature maps (in the paper's implementation details), with a full all-pairs dot-product cross-correlation matrix C in R^{HxWxHxW}, flattened into the cue.

Direction-aware Relationship: 16x16 feature maps and a correlation pyramid built by pooling the goal-side dimensions (3 layers). A 3x3 center-based lookup around each observation feature point at each scale gives multi-scale vectors, which are concatenated and fused by conv layers, then flattened.
Policy: a 2-layer GRU (embedding 128) with an actor-critic head takes the correlation cue and history.
Training: PPO with the ZER reward (distance and angle shaping, step penalty 0.01, and a final reward of 5 for stopping within the distance threshold plus 5 for a small angle), 400M steps on Gibson.

setting.backbone: ResNet-9 (shared, from scratch) + correlation module + 2-layer GRU actor-critic policy, trained with PPO

results: On Gibson, RSRNav reaches SPL 69.5 / SR 91.1 (agent-matched), beating FGPrompt-EF (66.5/90.4) and OVRL-V2 (58.7/82.0). Under user-matched goals it reaches 56.6/83.2 vs FGPrompt-EF 46.8/76.0. On MP3D and HM3D user-matched it gains about 12 and 6 SPL over FGPrompt, but its HM3D agent-matched SR (72.9) is below FGPrompt (74.2).
limitations: Trained and tested only in simulators, with no real-robot experiments; sim-to-real gap is acknowledged
Performance drops sharply under extreme goal-camera pitch (SR 40.2 in the extreme setting)
